title: U2’s The Edge Wrote an ‘Elf’ Sequel, But It ‘Petered Out and Never Happened,’ Says Andy Richter
description:
According to Andy Richter, U2’s the Edge penned a script for a sequel to “Elf” — but fans will likely never get to see (or read) it.

	On a recent
body:
According to Andy Richter, U2’s the Edge penned a script for a sequel to “Elf” — but fans will likely never get to see (or read) it.

	On a recent episode of “Obsessed: The Podcast,” the actor explained that Shauna Robertson, who’d produced the original film, once received a message saying that the band member, also known as David Howell Evans, had written a script for “Elf 2”


	“Somebody reached out to her and said, ‘The Edge from U2 has written a sequel to ‘Elf,’ and he wants to talk to you about it,’” Richter said. “It’s the weirdest story, but apparently it was fully written. Somewhere in the world there is an Edge-penned ‘Elf 2’ out there… I would love for that to make the light of day. It never happened. It’s one of those things where she’s like, ‘All right, sure, I’ll meet him,’ and then it just petered out and never happened.”
	

	In addition to the Edge, “Old School” and “The Hangover Part II” writer Scot Armstrong penned a separate sequel script about “the evil South Pole elves kidnapping Santa or something like that,” said Richter. (He also noted that Armstrong had helped write “Elf,” but wasn’t credited for guild and procedural reasons.)

	And yet despite how beloved the holiday classic remains 23 years later, Richter is steadfast in the belief that a sequel isn’t necessary at this point. “I’m on the side of ‘Let it stand,’” he said. ”Just let ‘Elf’ be ‘Elf.’ You don’t have to use every part of the animal.”

	He continued: “Now that time has passed, the movie has become so special that I think that people, rightfully so, are loath to mess with it because we all can think of movies that have been tarnished by their sequels. And this is so special and so perfect and so beloved… Why risk it?”
	

	“Elf,” directed by Jon Favreau, originally hit theaters in 2003, starring Will Ferrell, James Caan, Zooey Deschanel, Mary Steenburgen and others. The Christmas classic followed Buddy the elf (Ferrell), who travels from the North Pole to New York City to meet his biological father, Walter Hobbs (Caan).

	Ritcher appeared briefly in the film as one of Hobbs’ colleagues and co-wrote the book “Elf Unwrapped: Behind the Scenes of a Modern Christmas Classic,” released Tuesday.

schema.headline: U2’s The Edge Wrote an ‘Elf’ Sequel, But It ‘Petered Out and Never Happened,’ Says Andy Richter

title: Trump Offers Press Secretary Role to UFC CEO Dana White, Asks That He Bring Assistants to ‘Defend Us Against the Lunatic Left’
description: President Donald Trump has offered UFC President and CEO Dana White the White House press secretary role after Katie Zacharia was ousted in October
body:
President Donald Trump has offered UFC President and CEO Dana White the White House press secretary role after Katie Zacharia was ousted in October.

	“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Saturday. “I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris. We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job! President DONALD J. TRUMP”
	

	Though it’s unclear whether White has actually accepted the position — or just how serious Trump is about offering it to the executive — the news is the latest in recent events regarding potential press secretaries. Last week, Trump was asked during an interview whether musician Nikki Minaj would be considered for the position, to which he responded: “That’s a good idea. I think I’ll have to think about that… I’m going to think about that. How about you? You’d be pretty good, too,” he said.

	Zacharia served as Trump’s press secretary for just five days before she was let go — the shortest tenure in White House history. She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who held the position from Jan. 20, 2025 through Aug. 27. In Oct., she announced she was stepping down to join Fox News Channel as a contributor. At 27, she was the youngest person in American history to hold the position.
	

	UFC did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment.

schema.headline: Trump Offers Press Secretary Role to UFC CEO Dana White, Asks That He Bring Assistants to ‘Defend Us Against the Lunatic Left’

title: Bill Skarsgård Says He ‘Wasn’t Even Thrown Into the Mix’ to Be James Bond: ‘Maybe They Were Like, “We Can’t Do a Swede”’
description:
Bill Skarsgård won’t be the next 007, but he would play a Bond villain.

	In a recent appearance on Josh Horowitz’s “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, S
body:
Bill Skarsgård won’t be the next 007, but he would play a Bond villain.

	In a recent appearance on Josh Horowitz’s “Happy Sad Confused” podcast, Skarsgård revealed he wasn’t asked to test for Denis Villeneuve’s reboot. 

	“They didn’t call me about James Bond. I don’t know what that was about,” he joked. “Every single British, Australian [actor] … but maybe they were like, ‘We can’t do a Swede for this guy.’ I wasn’t even thrown into the mix.”
	

	Casting rumors for the new Bond have recently reached a fever pitch, with names like Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden swirling around. Most recently, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were revealed to have screen-tested for the role.

	Skarsgård agreed with Horowitz that he wouldn’t want to sign on for a decade plus of playing 007. “That’s right,” he said. “Just want to go in and do one Mads Mikkelsen villain.”

	“It’s not something that I’m actively looking for, but if I feel compelled to do something, yeah,” Skarsgård continued. “It’s the weird thing. A lot of people ask me, what goes into picking your roles or whatever and I don’t really know how to say it other than I feel drawn or compelled to. It’s something that you can’t really put your words on it and describe why it’s happening.”

	He added: “But I’ve also noticed that I don’t want to become jaded. Which means that I think I could probably go long stretches without working and waiting for something to be compelling enough for me to work on.”

	The Swedish actor is no stranger to a villainous character. He has played Pennywise in the “It” movies, Count Orlok in Robert Eggers’ “Nosferatu,” Eric Draven in “The Crow” and Marquis Vincent Bisset de Gramont in “John Wick: Chapter 4.” But he told Horowitz that he is becoming more discerning about the villain roles he takes on.
	

	“For a villain, it would have to be something that felt original to me, that was something that I hadn’t done before,” Skarsgård said. “I feel, kind of, spent with those things. But there are villains [that] could be really fun in different ways and if it’s the right kind.”

schema.headline: Bill Skarsgård Says He ‘Wasn’t Even Thrown Into the Mix’ to Be James Bond: ‘Maybe They Were Like, “We Can’t Do a Swede”’

title: French Cinema Is Thriving at Festivals but Facing an Uphill Battle in U.S. Theaters as Distributors Navigate a Shrinking Market
description: French cinema may be enjoying a golden run on the festival circuit and in the awards race, but getting those films into U.S. theaters, and persuadi
body:
French cinema may be enjoying a golden run on the festival circuit and in the awards race, but getting those films into U.S. theaters, and persuading American audiences to buy tickets, has become an increasingly uphill battle.

	That paradox was at the heart of a lively discussion at the American French Film Festival on Thursday, held in partnership with the CNC and Variety, where three veteran U.S. distributors painted a sobering picture of a market squeezed by shrinking theatrical opportunities.
	

	The panel brought together Robert Aronson, executive VP of Cohen Media Group; John Gerrans, co-president of Strand Releasing; and Paul Hudson, CEO of Outsider Pictures, who have collectively brought hundreds of international films to American audiences.

	The challenges extend well beyond French cinema. With fewer distributors acquiring independent films and arthouse theaters increasingly turning to mainstream Hollywood fare, even critically acclaimed movies are struggling to secure meaningful theatrical runs.

	The definition of a French-language box office hit has also changed dramatically along with the health of the special market for most foreign-language films. Jean-Pierre Jeunet’s cult film “Amélie” grossed approximately $33 million domestically a quarter-century ago. By comparison, Justine Triet’s Palme d’Or winner “Anatomy of a Fall,” one of the most successful French films of the last five years which was handled by Neon and won an Oscar, earned around $5 million in the U.S..

	The most accessible French blockbusters aren’t necessarily easier to market in the U.S. Samuel Goldwyn, whose company released Pathé’s two-part “The Three Musketeers” and “The Count of Monte Cristo,” and recently acquired Antonin Baudry’s historical epic saga “De Gaulle,” told Variety in a separate interview following the panel that these films have far broader commercial potential than their limited theatrical exposure suggests.
	

	“The only thing that makes it an arthouse movie is because it’s in a foreign language,” Goldwyn said of “De Gaulle,” adding that it could easily play on 1,000 screens if it were in English. He’s still managed to roll out the first opus of the WWII saga into theaters this weekend across key U.S. markets simultaneously with transactional VOD. 

	Yet while the pool of U.S. buyers has narrowed, competition remains fierce for the most coveted titles. Deep-pocketed players including Neon, Netflix, Mubi, A24 and Sony Pictures Classics continue to chase high-profile international films, particularly those from established auteurs. And even though Sony Pictures Classics, historically one of the most prolific U.S. buyers of French cinema, has become more selective, it’s still on the lookout for certain titles. The company just bought “Violette,” Jeunet’s latest film, and Louis Clichy’s animated feature “Iron Boy,” which won a prize at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard and was shortlisted as France’s Oscar submission alongside “De Gaulle.” The distributor also scored a solid theatrical run with Rebecca Zlotowski’s “A Private Life,” starring Jodie Foster, earlier this year.

	But for smaller distributors, competing for films with the greatest commercial potential is often a losing game.

	“We all see the same thing. So usually you go, boy, I could sell that. There’s something in here that I know I can sell. It’s got great reviews. It was in competition in Cannes or Berlin. And then Netflix buys it,” says Gerrans.

	In any case, securing screens can prove even harder than winning a bidding war. Arthouse theaters that once championed foreign-language cinema are increasingly booking Hollywood releases, while others have shuttered altogether.

	“We have to struggle to get into those theaters that used to be” devoted to arthouse films, Aronson said. Cohen Media Group owns the Landmark Theatres circuit, but that doesn’t guarantee bookings for its international releases. “They keep their own books and they have their own agenda and they need to be profitable,” said Aronson, whose recent acquisitions include László Nemes’ Cannes competition period drama “Moulin” and Géraldine Nakache’s “Think Good,” which played in Un Certain Regard.
	

	The company has also picked up Marc Fitoussi’s “All About Corinne,” starring Isabelle Huppert as a struggling film extra who dreams of becoming an actress and befriends a movie star played by Sandrine Kiberlain. Aronson, who compared the comedy’s tone to the French hit series “Call My Agent” (which was partly directed by Fitoussi), said star power remains a crucial selling point. 

	Strand has acquired Ulrike Ottinger’s experimental German-language vampire movie “The Blood Countess,” also starring Huppert, and Gerrans said her involvement has made a significant difference.

	“We’re able to book it because of her, and we’re getting a lot of festivals because of her,” Gerrans said. “So that one’s sort of booking itself, and that doesn’t happen too often.”

	For less recognizable titles, the outlook is considerably tougher. Gerrans admitted that he sometimes consults exhibitors before committing to acquisitions, particularly when sales agents require a theatrical release.

	“A lot of times we hold off and we ask some of the exhibitors, if I acquire this, will you play this film?” said Gerrans, whose upcoming French releases include “Flesh and Fuel” and “Daughters of Abraham.”

	He recalled pitching a film he loved to a New York exhibitor, only to be turned down. “It’s a fantastic film. You’ll love it. I think the audience will love it. They just go, that storyline seems a little too small.”

	Hudson, whose recent acquisitions include Cannes Un Certain Regard title “Congo Boy,” which earned Bradley Fiomona Dembeasset the best actor prize, described a similarly brutal scramble for screens.

	“We’re all trying to get the IFC Film Center or the Quad or the Angelika to book the film in New York, and there’s, I don’t know, 45 of us with all eight films trying to get them into these” theaters, Hudson joked.

	With major New York arthouse venues often booked months in advance, distributors sometimes resort to renting screens just to secure a theatrical launch.

	And competition isn’t coming only from Hollywood blockbusters. Repertory screenings, television series playing in multiplexes and special events are also taking up valuable screen space.

	“I understand arthouse theaters playing reissues,” Hudson said. “And young audiences rediscovering ‘Raise the Red Lantern.’ Amazing. But what about the new films? What about the new filmmakers? Where are the new ones going to get space to find room in the marketplace with all of this other stuff?”
	

	The squeeze extends beyond theaters. With DVD revenues largely gone, TV sales collapsing and streaming licenses losing value, independent distributors have fewer ways to recoup their investments.

	“We have a really hard time getting our films on the streaming platforms,” Aronson said. “Things have changed a lot in that market because they’re not that interested anymore in kind of single U.S.-only, after-theatrical streaming deals with independent distributors.”

	Hudson was particularly scathing about Amazon Prime’s declining royalty rates. “They were paying 10 cents per hour viewed, which is awful. But then they cut the rate down to 1 cent per hour viewed. Then they cut the rate down to half a cent per hour viewed.”

	He said he and other independent distributors have pulled titles from Amazon Prime and are looking to alternative outlets including Tubi, Roku, Pluto and YouTube.

	Strand operates its own subscription streaming channel through Amazon, but Gerrans said “they could decide tomorrow to turn it off.”

	With traditional distribution avenues under pressure, festivals are becoming an increasingly important way for films to reach audiences.

	“Film festivals are kind of like another tier of distribution, another level of distribution,” Aronson said. “It’s a way most independent films get seen by anyone.”

	Distributors are also looking to younger moviegoers, particularly through Letterboxd, which has built a passionate community of Gen Z cinephiles. But reaching that demographic without substantial marketing budgets remains a challenge.

	“Letterboxd is a real opportunity for us to find a younger audience,” Hudson said, describing how a friend’s son has helped him navigate the platform and build a community around his films.

	Yet enthusiasm for cinema doesn’t necessarily translate into ticket sales for contemporary French films.

	“I can’t even get my teenage kids to go see my movies,” Gerrans said, citing Strand’s release of Agathe Riedinger’s “Wild Diamond,” about a 17-year-old aspiring reality television star. Despite a premise seemingly tailored to younger audiences, the film failed to take off.

	Still, distributors are experimenting with ways to build word of mouth around films that might otherwise struggle to find an audience.
	

	Gerrans is optimistic about “Flesh and Fuel,” which he described as “the gay trucker movie you’ve never seen before,” betting that its uplifting ending will resonate with moviegoers.

	Hudson, meanwhile, plans an extended theatrical rollout for “Congo Boy,” stretching from Black History Month through Juneteenth, even if bookings remain scarce.

	“I can do five months because nobody’s clamoring for this movie to go onto a subscription service. But I may only get seven bookings.”

	French institutions including the CNC, Unifrance and Villa Albertine are also helping distributors promote French cinema through festivals, promotional events and talent travel.

	“All that helps to generate awareness,” Hudson said. “We have no support from the government. I mean, everything we do is from our own pockets. Film’s commerce here, it’s not culture.”

	The discussion was one of several panels bringing together French and American industry figures at the American French Film Festival, which is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year with a lineup of 60 films and series. The festival’s industry program also featured American filmmaker Randal Kleiser and French director Pierre Salvadori discussing artificial intelligence, as well as a panel moderated by Writers Guild of America West member Yvette Foy with French screenwriters Coralie Amedeo, Fanny Burdino, Abdel Raouf Dafri and Thomas Finkielkraut. The French delegation also included directors Baudry (“De Gaulle”), Laïla Marrakchi (“Strawberries”), Fitoussi (“All About Corinne”), Lukas Dhont (“Coward”) and actor-director Raphaël Quenard (“Le rêve américain”), among others.

schema.headline: French Cinema Is Thriving at Festivals but Facing an Uphill Battle in U.S. Theaters as Distributors Navigate a Shrinking Market

title: ‘Club Kid’ Scene-Stealer Kirby Howell-Baptiste on Playing a Drugged-Up Party Girl Who Turns Jordan Firstman’s World Upside Down: She’s ‘A Complete Tornado’
description:
“Should we do a bump?”

	It’s a line said, in various forms, numerous times across the first half of “Club Kid,” Jordan Firstman‘s hedonistic and h
body:
“Should we do a bump?”

	It’s a line said, in various forms, numerous times across the first half of “Club Kid,” Jordan Firstman‘s hedonistic and heartfelt coming-of-age comedy drama about a hard-partying New York club promoter suddenly forced to grapple with life and responsibilities. But the most hilariously-timed utterance comes in the middle of a crucial scene — one that shifts the entire movie — and from and by a minor, yet unforgettably wild, character.
	

	“She’s a massive party girl — she never sleeps, she only parties,” says Brit actor Kirby Howell-Baptiste of how Edison was described to her. “She’s completely lost all social boundaries. The lifetime of drugs melted half of her brain away, and all her social cues and etiquette have gone.”

	Howell-Baptiste’s etiquette-free Edison is only in “Club Kid” for a few minutes, but manages to steal the crucial scene in question from under the nose of writer, director and lead star Firstman.

	Roughly quarter of the way into the film, she rocks up unannounced and chaotic, sporting green braids and oversized sunglasses, at the apartment lived in by Firstman’s nightclub promoter Peter (Firstman), with 10-year-old Arlo (Reggie Absolom) in tow. While wandering around the place like it’s her own, she reveals — in a hysterically matter-of-fact manner — that not only is Arlo his, but she’s brought the kid across from the U.K. to live with him permanently. Boom.

	But Peter is gay — and confidently declares that he’s never slept with a woman. Not true, Edison asserts as she casually roams the kitchen on the hunt for literally anything remotely looking like drugs she can swallow or snort. He had sex with her friend Leonine a decade earlier at one of his nights while so high on ketamine, cocaine, GHB and (probably) more that he didn’t have a clue what was going on.
	

	“Nah, you fucked her, babes,” Edison says. “Point is, that’s your son.”

	Tragically, Leonine — as her apparent friend explains while sniffing some white powder she found on the counter — struggled with mental health issues (“She was in and out of the loony bin… what do you call it, rehab?”) and recently ended her life. “Last week she goes and tops herself — she fucking killed herself, babe.”

	In the midst of making these life-changing and upsetting revelations in the most wonderfully insensitive manner possible, Edison inquires if Peter and her should “do a bump” of coke (slightly shaken by how his life is quickly unravelling, he declines).

	“[Edison] is just a complete tornado,” says Londoner Howell-Baptiste, adding that she thinks the character is an “amalgamation of a few party people” Firstman has encountered. “But what I really love is that, although she’s absolutely bananas, she does feel quite real and quite relatable. I think everyone knows that person, to some degree. At some point in your life, you have met that person.” 

	Edison isn’t seen again in “Club Kid” after the apartment scene, in which she eventually leaves Arlo in Peter’s care and — predictably — fails to return to collect him as promised later on. But as Peter begins a frantic search to find her across various New York house parties, further levels of her comically debauched behaviour come to light, as he hears how she was kicked out of several places for simply being too much of a tornado to handle. 

	“I wasn’t part of those scenes, obviously, but what was really cool was that you got more of a picture of Edison,” she says. “Even in her absence, you got more of a picture of what she was doing and how she was just belligerently running around New York, hoovering up drugs at everyone’s party.”



	

					Kirby Howell-Baptiste as Edison in ‘Club Kid’
	



	Howell-Baptiste admits she had no idea who Firstman was when she was originally invited to audition for “Club Kid” in mid 2025. As someone who’s “not really on social media much” she missed his breakout during the COVID-19 pandemic. But she checked out some of his Instagram videos and thought he was funny. Crucially, the casting was being done by Carmen Cuba, who she says has “really exquisite taste” and thought, while she hadn’t seen the full script, the role seemed fun — “and the character was a party girl and I felt like I could channel that pretty well.” 
	

	A few months later, shooting in New York, Howell-Baptiste still didn’t have a full picture of what “Club Kid” was all about (she admits to only watching it in September), but her main takeaway was that Edison was written by someone “who knows how to party.”

	While the scene they shot was “almost verbatim” from the audition, there was a bit of ad-libbing, with Howell-Baptiste being the one who added the British slang term “tops herself.”

	“And afterwards, everyone was like, ‘What do you you mean ‘”tops herself”?’ Because, obviously, we’re in a film that’s written by a gay man. There’s so much about it that celebrates queer culture, and topping has a completely different meaning there,” she says. Despite offering to remove the word, she was told to keep it in. “It made the cut — and it think it’s really fun and adds even more confusion when it comes to American audiences being like: ‘What is going on with this girl?'”

	In terms of notes from Firstman, she says the main discussion was how he wanted Edison’s voice to sound, with the request that — alongside the British accent — she was “very hoarse, like she’s been up all night and almost always lost her voice.”

	To achieve this, Howell-Baptiste channelled former Spice Girl Mel B. “She always had this slight hoarseness singing that I always thought was very cool, so that’s where my mind went,” she says.

	Having shot her key scene (and the even shorter scene in which Edison and Leonine first meet Peter in the club) in the fall of 2025, Howell-Baptiste — whose long line of credits include “Killing Eve,” “Barry” and “Hacks” — moved on to other acting jobs. Several months later, while filming Season 3 of British TV drama “Sherwood,” Firstman messaged her to tell her that “Club Kid” had been accepted into Cannes. “I was like, ‘How incredible,’ but that was sort of it for me for a very long time.”

	Of course, “Club Kid” wound up being the talk of the festival festival, the breakout hit that sparked an intense bidding war eventually won by A24 for the princely sum of $17 million. Howell-Baptiste was oblivious to it all (“I joke that I live under a rock”) until her manager messaged her saying “Are you aware of everything that’s going on with ‘Club Kid’ in Cannes?” Keeping with the theme, it was a makeup artist who later informed her that “Club Kid” was going to Toronto. “I just wasn’t aware of any of the buzz!”
	

	Thankfully, Howell-Baptiste was able to attend the premiere at the BFI London Film Festival and took to the stage at the Royal Festival Hall with Firstman and Absolom, staying to watch the film to experience the laughs, cheers and tears from a hugely enthusiastic audience. Now, she can finally enjoy having a crucial — and spectacularly funny — role in one of the standout movies of the year.

	“I filmed in a complete vacuum — I just did one scene with three other characters and filmed the party scene, which was just one night,” she says. “So it’s all come as a really pleasant surprise to me — it’s lovely.”

schema.headline: ‘Club Kid’ Scene-Stealer Kirby Howell-Baptiste on Playing a Drugged-Up Party Girl Who Turns Jordan Firstman’s World Upside Down: She’s ‘A Complete Tornado’

title: ‘Full House’ Star Jodie Sweetin Says She Had ‘$190 in My Bank Account’ Before Filming ‘Fuller House’: ‘I Had to Borrow Money the First Week’
description: Jodie Sweetin, who first shot to fame as Stephanie Tanner on the beloved sitcom “Full House,” is opening up about her financial struggles over the
body:
Jodie Sweetin, who first shot to fame as Stephanie Tanner on the beloved sitcom “Full House,” is opening up about her financial struggles over the years, particularly how close she came to running out of funds before returning to the show’s 2016 reboot, “Fuller House.”

	“I had to borrow money the first week I was working on ‘Fuller House,’ and I [skittered] into my first paycheck with like $190 in my bank account,” Sweetin revealed on a recent episode of the “We’re Still Here, Babe” podcast. “And nobody that I worked with knew that.”
	

	Sweetin has been open about her struggles with addiction, and also discussed how those habits left her with “no money” at a certain point, leading her to broaden her employment search to non-Hollywood gigs. “I didn’t have [an] ego about it,” Sweetin said. “I didn’t care that I was, quote, unquote, working a normal job. I think other people again were like, ‘What are you doing here?’ And I was like, ‘Paying my bills. Kids don’t pay for themselves.’”

	She continued: “And not like I was ever a materialistic person, but you learn humility when you are at Target, and you’ve got to turn around and, you know, put some shit back, because you don’t have the money on your debit card.”

	“Full House” ran for eight seasons, from 1987 to 1995. “Fuller House” ran for five seasons on Netflix, totalling nearly 80 episodes. Original cast members, including Candace Cameron Bure, Andrea Barber, Scott Weinger, Bob Saget, Lori Loughlin, Dave Coulier and John Stamos, all returned for the series. (Notably absent were Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen.) Juan Pablo Di Pace, Adam Hagenbuch, John Brotherton, Michael Campion, Elias Harger and Soni Bringas also starred in the reboot.

schema.headline: ‘Full House’ Star Jodie Sweetin Says She Had ‘$190 in My Bank Account’ Before Filming ‘Fuller House’: ‘I Had to Borrow Money the First Week’

title: Oscar Short Film Race Spotlights Bold Stories, New Animation Tech and Creative Risk-Taking
description: Some of the most compelling stories in contention for the Academy Awards aren’t unfolding across two or three hours. They’re being told in a fractio
body: Some of the most compelling stories in contention for the Academy Awards aren’t unfolding across two or three hours. They’re being told in a fraction of that time. The race in the short film categories is taking shape, offering a showcase for emerging filmmakers, well-known talents and storytellers pushing the boundaries of what can be accomplished in 40 minutes or less.Spanning live action, animation and documentary filmmaking, the short film categories have long served as a launching pad for directors and a creative outlet for industry veterans eager to experiment outside the constraints of feature-length filmmaking.Short films often operate with modest budgets and limited — if any — distribution. But those constraints can also encourage creative risk-taking, resulting in intimate character studies, groundbreaking animation and documentaries that tackle volatile subjects with remarkable economy.Anne Sundberg, helmer of “A Month in Minnesota,” a documentary that chronicles the fallout from the fatal ICE shootings in Minneapolis, wanted her film to show the community response to this violence.“The first thing was I really wanted to bring people inside the experience of what it was to be in Minnesota at the time that this happened,” says Sundberg. “There were networks that developed. There was a clear sense of purpose. This could have been any city in the U.S. and it happened in Minneapolis, and it was a normal city where kids went to the park and played, where people felt safe going to school, where people generally felt pretty safe going to work, and it turned in a moment. And I think what you saw happen in Minnesota was that people learned quickly how to form networks how to trust each other, how to figure out who needed what.”Short documentaries can also zoom in on one person and their unique struggles, as in “Listen,” directed by Taliesin Black-Brown, who followed sound recordist Hank Lentfer as he documented sounds in nature as he cares for his mother, who’s in the final stages of dementia.“It’s my real hope that it just inspires people to listen, to maybe pause and then to kind of just experience nature and the sounds around them,” says Black-Brown. “It can be profound to experience those sounds and I think sometimes there’s so much noise in our environment, whether it’s the noise in urban places, or someone is doing construction over there. Just to make space to sit in a park and listen to a bird. It can be really healing.”Some of this year’s early frontrunners in the animated shorts category come from the singular visions of directors committed to a genre or experimenting with new technologies. Short films are often a place for new animation techniques to be given an opportunity to be used in surprising ways.For the director of “Praying Mantis,” it was a way to bring his love of hand-drawn 2D animation together with his passion for horror films. Helmer Joe Hsieh spent about four years bringing this project to the screen.“I think short films are a very, very good way to show that horror and animation are full of imagination,” says Hsieh, who is based in Taiwan. “A short film is also a good way to show that you can make what you imagined into something. You start with the idea of the character and you build from there to make a story for the audiences.”With “Dear Upstairs Neighbors,” the filmmakers wanted to push emerging AI technologies to take artist-created drawings and assemble a short based on those drawings while guided by the artists. The movie follows a frazzled insomniac as she tries to get some sleep.Marcia Mayer, executive producer of the short who formerly worked at Pixar, sees the controversy around AI as similar to what happened when CG tech came along and disrupted the hand-drawn pipeline.“Short films are often done as a test of new technology in animation,” says Mayer. “We scanned 35 paintings and trained a model on the different styles of painting. We’re using AI to create the look the filmmakers always wanted and it’s making it possible to make this film in a realistic timeline. It became possible for Connie [He], the director, to use these tools to make the film she wanted to make.”In the live action category, the landscape is also diverse, with filmmakers sometimes taking inspiration from their own lives or even coming to subjects after they’re commissioned to create a short.“Jozefa,” helmed by Kathryn Kalucki, was crafted as a short after the filmmakers had looked for a way to create a story about the director’s grandmother and her early experiences as a refugee.“My producing partner and I decided we had to use the resources we have, the talent we have and the time we have to create a short,” says Kalucki. “We shot for a very feverish two-and-a-half days, and we had a one-week prep. We shot in Burbank and we were able to make something powerful, even with all those limitations.”Filmmakers who create short films are often pushing against limited resources and abbreviated shooting schedules, but for creators like Patrick Willems, who directed the live action short “Power Trip,” that’s not new. It may actually even be a bit easier to work with a crew who are used to moving quickly to capture what they need over just a few days.“I make YouTube videos for a living, and I have a channel where I do long-form film criticism, but I also weave in narrative filmmaking into everything,” says Willems. “I’m used to having almost no resources and having to do everything myself. So making a short like this feels amazing because I don’t have to do everything myself and there’s a great professional crew working with me. You learn there’s no time to waste.”Mekhai Lee, who directed the live action short “Them That’s Not,” also sees the short as a unique art form and not necessarily a bid to a feature. There are advantages for him to tell his stories in this way.“It’s like the novella to the novel,” says Lee. “I like the short story. I love reading short stories by [James] Baldwin. I love Octavia Butler. I just finished a series of short stories by her. And these are novelists. The short films just work in a different way. There’s a different approach to it. I think the way that this film was executed in this time, in this space, within these parameters, that is exactly what and how it needed to be done. This is exactly the best way to put the story into the world.”Seasoned filmmakers like Academy Award-winning Sean Baker (“Anora”) find making a short an opportunity to explore themes and develop techniques that have interested them. His live action short, “Sandiwara,” stars Oscar-winner Michelle Yeoh, and is the fruit of fashion house Self-Portrait’s residency program.“I think you have to always be practicing your craft and learning new things,” says Baker. “I never consider myself an expert filmmaker. So, when these opportunities come around and I connect with the idea, it’s just an opportunity for further learning and it was wonderful to connect with a new crew that worked on this short.”Filmmaker Maggie Gyllenhaal has a couple of features and a lot of acclaim on her resumé, and views shorts as a type of art that gives a voice to projects not always meant to be developed as features. Her live action short, “Flesh Impact,” focuses on the life of Marilyn Monroe and stars Ellen Burstyn and Dakota Johnson.“I think some stories are meant to be 17 minutes, like mine,” says Gyllenhaal, who was commissioned by Genesis to create a short film about Monroe. “Short films don’t get distribution. It’s not realistic to finance something like this. I think it’s an interesting medium that isn’t totally rooted in commercialism.But where does this live? I think of short films almost like these little geodes that look like a rock from the outside but when you turn it over it’s full of something unexplainable.”

schema.headline: Oscar Short Film Race Spotlights Bold Stories, New Animation Tech and Creative Risk-Taking

title: Richard Lloyd, Television’s Fiery and Fluent Guitarist, Dies at 75
description: Richard Lloyd, whose fluent and fiery guitar work was a vital element in the influential 1970s-era New York City band Television, died on Saturday
body:
Richard Lloyd, whose fluent and fiery guitar work was a vital element in the influential 1970s-era New York City band Television, died on Saturday at his home in Chattanooga, Tenn., according to the New York Times. The cause of death was bile duct cancer; he was 75.

	While commonly associated with the punk rock movement of the era, Television’s sound was anything but punk, driven by Lloyd and frontman Tom Verlaine’s intricate and virtuosic soloing, unusual song structures and Verlaine’s low-key and deadpan vocals. The band’s classic 1977 album “Marquee Moon” is a defining document of the era, including such oft-covered songs as “See No Evil” and the nearly 11-minute title track and casting a vast influence on future alternative rockers like R.E.M. and Sonic Youth.
	

	Yet Television’s peak era was brief, lasting for just two albums before the band split in 1978 and Verlaine and Lloyd pursued solo careers, although the band reformed in 1992 and regrouped several times over the years.

	While Verlaine, who died in 2023, is commonly recognized as the band’s frontman and auteur, Lloyd’s contributions were perennially underrated. The pair’s styles were complimentary and in many ways similar, but, broadly speaking, Lloyd brought the fire and Verlaine the finesse. While his struggles with mental health and substance abuse unquestionably marred his career, in addition to his blazing work with Television, Lloyd released nine solo albums and contributed fiery work to Matthew Sweet’s classic 1991 album “Girlfriend,” which also featured fellow CBGB-era guitar master Robert Quine.
	

	Ironically, Television, which formed in 1973, were the band to initiate the Lower Manhattan club CBGB, which proved to be the key incubator for punk rock. According to legend, Verlaine and Lloyd were walking past the venue, saw owner Hilly Kristal outside and asked what kind of music the venue showcased. Told “Country, Bluegrass and Blues,” hence the club’s title, the pair replied that their band played something like that (it did not).

	Yet the group secured a booking, other groups like the Ramones, Blondie and Talking Heads soon followed suit, and by 1975 CBGB was the hotbed of a scene and sound that would eventually revolutionize rock music.

	Lloyd was born Richard John Alt on Oct. 25, 1951, in Pittsburgh, Lloyd moved with his mother to New York City as an infant. He grew up in Greenwich Village, took up the guitar at an early age and attended concerts at the legendary Fillmore East as a teen; his struggles with mental health and substance abuse also began at this time. He attended New York’s prestigious Stuyvesant High School but dropped out before graduation.

	After living briefly in Boston and Los Angeles, he returned to New York and gravitated toward the burgeoning scene around punk forerunners the New York Dolls. Verlaine and his longtime friend Richard Hell had formed a band called the Neon Boys with drummer Billy Ficca, and, after being introduced through Terry Ork (who would later release Television’s first single, “Little Johnny Jewel” on his self named independent label), brought Lloyd into the band. Hell left in 1975 and was replaced by Blondie bassist Fred Smith, raising the band’s instrumental prowess significantly.

	Things progressed quickly for the band from there — David Bowie famously called Television “the most original band I’ve seen in New York” — and the band signed with Elektra Records in 1976 and released “Marquee Moon” in February of 1977. Domestic sales were unimpressive but the band, and the scene, captured the imaginations of the influential British rock music press — where punk rock was exploding — and the band actually enjoyed three hit singles, successful tours and two top 10 albums in the U.K.

	However, the success was short-lived, as the band — marred by Lloyd’s debilitating heroin addiction — split shortly after the released of its second album, “Adventure.” Despite that, an album titled “Live at the Old Waldorf,” recorded in June of 1978 shortly before the band’s dissolution, finds them at the peak of their powers.
	

	Lloyd regrouped the following year and released his first solo album, “Alchemy,” and played on albums by X’s John Doe as well as Sweet. In 1992, at the height of their alt-rock-era influence, Television reformed, released a self-titled album and toured. They regrouped multiple times over the ensuing years, although usually without Lloyd, whose relationship with Verlaine continued to be fractious. Yet there’s little question that Television and Lloyd had long since made their mark on the history of rock music.

title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Takashi Yamazaki Dreamed of Seeing His Hometown Destroyed by King Ghidorah. He Finally Made It Happen.
description: It’s been just over two years since “Godzilla Minus One” collected the Oscar in visual effects. Writer, director and VFX supervisor Takashi Yamazak
body:
It’s been just over two years since “Godzilla Minus One” collected the Oscar in visual effects. Writer, director and VFX supervisor Takashi Yamazaki became the first helmer to receive a VFX trophy since Stanley Kubrick for 1968’s “2001: A Space Odyssey.”

	Reflecting on that historic night, Yamazaki, speaking through a translator, said, “It was just such a shock to us. I never thought that would happen in a million years because here we are on the other side of the planet making movies for our domestic market.” He continued, “That people in Hollywood even saw the movie, let alone give it a nomination and responded to that, shows how open-minded the Academy is to different types of films.” He said the win opened up “doors, options and possibilities for my career.”
	

	One of those doors opening is “Godzilla Minus Zero.” Now in theaters, the sequel picks up in 1949, two years after the tumultuous events of “Godzilla Minus One,” and continues the story of the Shikishima family as they face “an all-new calamity.”

	It is the 38th film in the Godzilla franchise and the 34th produced by Toho, the Japanese entertainment company that originally created the franchise. Yamazaki returns to both the director’s chair and as VFX supervisor. The sequel stars Kamiki Ryunosuke and Hamabe Minami and marks the first time a Japanese feature has been shot for Imax screens.

	Yamazaki discussed the film and why bringing one of his favorite kaiju, King Ghidorah, to the big screen in this installment fulfills a childhood dream.
	
		How did you balance telling this story with the biggest, loudest action sequences, but at the core, keep it deeply emotional?	

	I wanted to make sure that what’s happening on the human layer and what was happening on the kaiju and Godzilla layer were not separate from each other. It was important that the actions taken by humans affect the actions that the kaiju take, and vice versa. How the kaiju responds then causes the humans to act in a certain way. So the two are intertwined. It was important for the engagement and the immersion that all aspects of the story are affecting each other.
	
	
		How did you come up with the title ‘Godzilla Minus Zero,’ and what does “zero” mean in the context of this film?	

	Zero represents this idea of neutrality. Our characters have an ordinary life, which, given the period and what’s happening in the film, is hard to attain. After “Godzilla Minus One,” I felt that this family attained that only to be faced with a new tragedy that’s pulling all of these humans apart from each other.

	In certain disciplines of math, there is a difference between putting the negative sign in front of zero and what it represents is this idea of approaching zero. That’s exactly what the characters in this film are doing. They’re trying to claw their way back to what feels neutral — an ordinary life — after being thrown into this massive tragedy.



	

	


	
		There are so many great sequences in the film. One key moment is when Godzilla emerges for the first time and rises out of the water as the seaplane is taking off. I read that it took 2 billion water particle visual effects shots. Can you discuss what it took from page to screen to pull that off?	

	The screenplay says something along the lines of “Godzilla emerges from the ocean and chases the seaplane.” But I also do the storyboarding for the film myself. When I was trying to compose the shot, I opted for a long-lens type of visual effect shot because Godzilla in this film is 50.1 meters tall (164 feet). If you line up the different Godzilla movies, Godzilla is on the smaller side. By compressing the depth of field with a long lens, we could create the illusion of Godzilla’s size.

	The seaplane is trying to take off, headed toward the camera. So there’s a lot of forward movement. We get to see the waves behind the seaplane, and the waves are Godzilla emerging from the ocean, trying to mount the plane. If it does, it’s over for everyone. The long lens certainly helped create and amplify that drama.
	

	The shot turned out even better than I had imagined thanks to the wonderful team that we have doing VFX. This particular scene was important to me because it’s the first time we see a full frontal view of Godzilla emerging from the ocean. It took a lot of time to render all those particles. It was important that we spent a lot of our resources, time, and rendering power on this shot because of how crucial it is for the audience to feel that threat.



	

	


	
		King Ghidorah is a big part of the Godzilla lore, and it was fantastic seeing your vision of this character. What was it like for you to bring this character to life in your film?	

	When Ghidorah made its silver screen debut in “Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster,” it was the first kaiju to appear in Matsumoto City, the same city where I was born and raised. I was very excited to go to the movie theater and see Ghidorah smash up my hometown. But when I got to the theater and saw the film, Ghidorah flies over Matsumoto Castle, and that was it. So I was disappointed.

	With “Godzilla Minus One,” I was able to make the movie I wanted to see as a child. King Ghidorah appears in Matsumoto City, which is the same city where I set that scene, and it smashes it up. It’s really a dream come true for me. At the same time, I really love King Ghidorah as a kaiju because the design is amazing.
	



	

	


	
		There’s an emotional sequence with the young child Akiko crying that involves her parents. What was it like shooting that and getting the actress to cry for so long in the way that she did?	

	We shot “Godzilla Minus One,” and Akiko (Sae Nagatani) was 2 years old. Every time she was about to cry and get cranky, that’s when we would run in with the cameras and the actors and begin shooting. She’s 5 years old now, and if we explain scenes, she has a very good understanding of what we are trying to do and gives us the type of reactions we’re looking for. Without too much explanation on my part, she was able to give us the performance. It felt very authentic.



	

	


	
		Given you did all the storyboards, what was the most satisfying scene or sequence for you to pull off?	

	You see it in the trailer: there’s a mother and a baby in the house, and they’ve been levitated by Ghidorah’s gravity beam, and then they fall. This shot came out brilliantly. At first, I was struggling, trying to figure out how we would shoot this. We built the set, and this piece had a little bit of a tilt to it. We used drones to shoot around it, so we had our visuals, which we fleshed out with VFX. It’s a very scary and violent scene, and it tells us a lot about King Ghidorah’s power. It also serves as an indirect expression of how much terror and fear it can incite within people.
	
		Do you have another Godzilla movie in you?	

	Let’s all stay excited for the third installment of this franchise …

	This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

schema.headline: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Takashi Yamazaki Dreamed of Seeing His Hometown Destroyed by King Ghidorah. He Finally Made It Happen.

title: Keira Knightley and ‘Black Doves’ Creator Joe Barton  Why Helen Should Have Been the One to Kill [SPOILER], That Oner and Hopes for Season 3
description:
Nov 7, 2026 11:00am PT	
	

	
		Keira Knightley and ‘Black Doves’ Creator Joe Barton  Why Helen Should Have Been the One to Kill [SPO
body:
Nov 7, 2026 11:00am PT	
	

	
		Keira Knightley and ‘Black Doves’ Creator Joe Barton  Why Helen Should Have Been the One to Kill [SPOILER], That Oner and Hopes for Season 3
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Courtesy of Matthew Towers/Netfl
	

		
	
				


	SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “Black Doves” Season 2, now streaming on Netflix.

	Keira Knightley is back as super spy Helen Webb in Season 2 of “Black Doves,” alongside Ben Whishaw as her troubled colleague Sam Young and Sarah Lancashire as her stoic spymaster Reed.

	The show, created by Joe Barton, returns with plenty of action, blood and bodies as Reed goes missing, Sam makes a Faustian pact with a shady benefactor and Helen’s secret identity is almost exposed — a threat that’s all the more serious given her new role in Number 10 Downing Street now that her husband, Wallace (Andrew Buchan), has become Prime Minister.



	

					Sarah Lancashire and Ben Whishaw 
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	With Season 2 out now on Netflix, Knightley and Barton sat down with Variety to discuss why the showrunner chose to focus on Reed’s backstory this season, how the series differs from Apple TV’s London spy thriller “Slow Horses” — and the one character Knightley really wanted to kill.


	
		We still don’t know a lot about Helen’s backstory by the end of Season 1, but Season 2 focuses on Reed’s. Why did you decide to shift the focus this season?	

	Joe Barton: It organically came out the storytelling process of Reed’s backstory, and the idea of the sins of the past coming forward and everyone suffering for them. And I wanted to do a “Berlin in the ‘80s” spy thing.


	
		We do get a flashback of Helen just after she’s given birth and is trying to balance parenthood, marriage, friendship and her career (one that involves killing people). How do you have such good insight into motherhood, Joe?	

	Barton: My partner tells me every day.

	Keira Knightley: I was gonna say, I think you’ve got a front row seat to that one.



	

					Keira Knightley 
									Courtesy of Netflix
	


	
		The line when Helen is lamenting having to kill Marie (Molly Chesworth), and she says “Do you know how hard it is to find a good nanny?” rang particularly true.	

	Knightley: [Joe] handed me the script that [said] “You’re shooting the nanny,” and I was like, “But she stays late, what the fuck are you talking about? You don’t shoot her! She never goes home — this is the childcare of dreams.” But she has taken the kids, so we do have to kill the nanny. So we did have that conversation.


	
		There’s also the scene in which Helen is about to shoot Franz (Rainer Wöss), and her breasts start leaking because she’s still breastfeeding, which mirrors a scene in Season 1 when Helen is shooting assassins while heavily pregnant. How much are you thinking about that juxtaposition of mother and mercenary when you’re preparing for the role?	

	Knightley: That’s what I love about it, because life doesn’t stop just because you’ve got other stuff. I think that’s what’s lovely about the whole show, is that as heightened and — I mean this in the best way — ridiculous as the whole thing is, it equally has that very human part of it, and that’s what makes it great, in my opinion. That’s what makes it really fun, and that’s what makes it really interesting.


	
		The heightened reality is definitely a talking point, especially now Helen is the prime minister’s wife. For example when she’s walking around without a security detail —	

	Barton: She doesn’t have it [in real life].

	Knightley: Oh yeah, you did actually do that research.

	Barton: The prime minister’s wife doesn’t get a security detail, so it’s very realistic.



	

					Ben Whishaw and Keira Knightley 
									Courtesy of Matthew Towers/Netflix
	




	
		I didn’t know that! What about nobody recognizing her as she’s fighting her way through Somerset House?	

	Knightley: She’s got a hat and glasses, come on. It’s fine!



	
		How much are you trying to balance the action pieces with reality?	

	Knightley: [To Barton] How much are we balancing reality?

	Barton: Well, it’s a tricky balancing act, isn’t it?

	Knightley: Yes, it is.

	Barton: I would say we’re not always balancing it.

	Knightley: It’s a foot off the floor. A good foot off the floor, sometimes two feet off the floor.

	Barton: A couple of meters off the floor! We get talked about a lot with “Slow Horses,” because obviously [they’re both] London spy shows. I think the big difference between us and them is ostensibly “Slow Horses” takes place in the real world, and I don’t think we do. There are obviously recognizable elements of the real world, but fundamentally it’s more me taking a chapter out of the James Bond or “Mission Impossible” book, where you can have these almost flights of fantasy. We have our cake and eat it too, basically.

	Knightley: That’s the idea, isn’t it.

	Barton: With the prime minister’s wife, my argument is always I don’t actually know what Keir Starmer’s wife looks like.

	Knightley: When we were shooting, it was Keir Starmer’s wife [Starmer resigned in June], and we were all like, “Actually, I don’t know her name particularly, and I don’t know what she looks like.” So we were all very pleased about that, because we were like, “See? She could be doing anything.”


	Barton: She could be a spy.



	

					Andrew Buchan and Keira Knightley
									Courtesy of Matthew Towers/Netflix
	




	
		Keira, at the end of Season 1 your one request to Joe was that you wanted to kill Dani (Agnes O’Casey) because, as you said, “I don’t think it’s OK that she tried to fuck my husband and kill me on Christmas Eve.” But in Season 2, he gives that honor to Gabrielle Creevy (Eleanor) who lobs a grenade into the elevator.	

	Knightley: I didn’t get to, no — he made me shoot the nanny instead! I was like, “That’s not the one I want to kill. I want to kill Dani! Why didn’t you let me kill Dani? You killed Dani, and you didn’t let me do it.”

	Barton: Do you know what that was? I wanted to keep Dani alive so that you could kill her, [but] it didn’t make sense to get your character there. But then I was on set with Aggie and we were talking. I was like, “I love working with you, and I think the character is so interesting and there could be more.” And she’s like, “Oh no, the thing is, I’ve just got this new job, so I wouldn’t even be available for another series.” 

	It’s like, huh. Catch a grenade!


	
		You also killed off Neve Campbell, who played presidential aide Cecile. Did you consider bringing her back for another season?	

	Barton: I just thought it would be so shocking to do that to poor Neve.

	Knightley: I didn’t see that coming. Another one bites the dust.



	

					Ambika Mod and Keira Knightley 
									Courtesy of Matthew Towers/Netflix
	




	
		The scene with Ambika Mod (Laila) where you’re being chased through Somerset House was quite ambitious. What was that like to shoot?	

	Knightley: We didn’t have a lot of time to rehearse that sequence, and all of a sudden, Julian [Farino, the director] said, “Actually, I want to shoot it in a oner.” And me and Ambika were like, “But we haven’t learnt the fight, so how are you going to shoot it in a oner?” And [the crew] were like, “Well — good luck! We’ll just try and make it work!” So it was quite an interesting day. We did actually manage to shoot it in a oner.


	
		How many takes did you get?	

	Knightley: Five.

	Barton: It ended up working really well, but it wasn’t always a guarantee, was it?

	Knightley: It did end up working out well. It definitely didn’t feel like a guarantee on the day that it would.


	
		Season 1 was very much a Christmas show, and Joe said everyone felt a bit “Christmased out” by the end. This season, there’s just a little nod to Christmas at the end. Was that deliberate?	

	Barton: Yeah, we have bits of Christmas. We pop in and out of it.

	Knightley: We were shooting over Christmas again, which meant that it was quite hard to avoid at certain points. But actually, when we finally shot in Trafalgar Square, it was post-Christmas, so we did then have to invent the Christmas tree.

	Barton: We had to digitally put the tree in. The first [season] we were chasing Christmas, and this one we were running from it. The [real] tree is quite threadbare, so we were like “We could make it even nicer,” and the Norwegian government [who give the Trafalgar Square Christmas tree to the U.K. each year] were like “No, you’re not allowed to, it has to look like [the real thing].”


	
		Oh wow. You had to get approval from the Norwegian government for the digital tree?	

	Barton: Yeah it has to be the same type of tree and you’re not allowed to make it too –

	Knightley: — too bushy.
	
		Is there going to be a Season 3?	

	Barton: I’m in a writers’ room for it at the moment, and we’re hoping.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.



	
		More from Variety

schema.headline: Keira Knightley and ‘Black Doves’ Creator Joe Barton  Why Helen Should Have Been the One to Kill [SPOILER], That Oner and Hopes for Season 3

title: Dad Allegedly Left Sleeping Daughter Outside Target to Save Spot in Line for Pokémon Cards

                          Allegedly Left Daughter at Target to Save S
body:
South Carolina Dad Arrested
                          Allegedly Left Daughter at Target to Save Spot in Pokémon Card Line
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 7, 2026
                            2:20 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            One father proved that you really don't gotta catch 'em all ... after being accused of leaving his sleeping 6-year-old daughter outside a Target to stand in line for Pokémon cards.
      
    
            John-Michael Dooley was arrested on Nov. 6 ... after witnesses claimed he left his daughter outside the store with a pillow and blanket at 1 AM and didn't return for over an hour ... the Charlestown PD shared.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            After witnesses called the cops, Dooley eventually strolled up and was arrested around 2:30 AM ... this, according to CPD.
      

            Once placed in custody, police say that Dooley 'fessed up to leaving her behind to keep his place in line and returning home.
      
    
            Dooley has been charged with unlawful conduct toward a child and is being held at the Al Cannon Detention Center.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Thankfully enough, his kid was unharmed ... and placed into emergency protective custody with social services.
      
    
            With his bond being set at $40,000, he's set to appear in court on Dec. 18 ... according to court records.

                                                                        Published 
                              November 7, 2026
                            9:20 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 7, 2026
                                2:58 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
          UPDATE
  
    
            11:45 AM PT -- Małopolska Police have said in an update that four women and two men are among those killed in today's attack and that officers responded to the incident within 23 seconds.
      
    
            At least 6 people are dead after a gunman opened fire from his car at a busy marketplace in Krakow, Poland.
      
    
            Around a dozen people -- including police officers -- were treated for injuries after the deadly shooting that ended with the gunman being shot ... the Małopolska Police shared on social media.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The unidentified suspect was then taken to a nearby hospital ... it's unclear what his current status is.
      

            In an update, police confirmed that the suspect is a Polish citizen and denied reports of a second suspect.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The shooting happened around 3 PM ... when the suspect drove onto Rynek Glowny square before opening fire on the crowd and a tram ... according to Krakow’s public transportation operator, MPK Krakow.
      
    
            MPK wrote on X ... "According to the information we have, neither the passengers nor the driver were injured."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            This story is developing ... we'll keep you posted as we learn more.
